intro: Seven seals, seven trumpets, seven bowls: twenty-one judgements at the heart of Revelation. Are they a future seven-year catastrophe, a map of church history, timeless symbols, or the judgement Jesus foretold on the generation that rejected him? This study lays all twenty-one on one board, traces their roots in the plagues of Egypt and the prophets, matches them with the record of the Jewish war of AD 66-70, and shows where other readings run into trouble. It follows the partial preterist reading, with the best case for each other view given beside it.
orthodoxy: Partial preterists hold that Revelation was written before AD 70 and that most of its judgements fell on Jerusalem and its persecutors in that generation, while Christ's bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement (Revelation 20:11-15) remain future. Futurist, historicist and idealist readers are fellow believers; their arguments are given fairly here. The matches with history are proposed correspondences, not claims that every detail is literal.

bookends.words: Things that must soon take place
Even those who pierced him will see him; all the tribes of the land will wail
Do not seal up the words of the prophecy, for the time is near

series.image: White horse, a bow and a crown
series.fulfilled: Conquest begins: Christ going out conquering, or Rome's armies setting out under Vespasian. Either way, the war on the land is launched.
series.futurist: The Antichrist's rise, conquering by false peace at the start of the tribulation.

series.image: Red horse; peace taken from the land
series.fulfilled: War and civil strife: Josephus describes Jews killing one another in every city and faction fighting in Jerusalem.
series.futurist: Worldwide war in the future tribulation.

series.image: Black horse; a day's wage for a quart of wheat
series.fulfilled: Famine prices in the siege: Josephus records people selling all they had for a measure of grain.
series.futurist: Global famine and economic collapse.

series.image: Pale horse: Death and Hades over a fourth of the land
series.fulfilled: Sword, famine, plague and beasts, Ezekiel's four judgements on Jerusalem (Ezekiel 14:21), across a quarter of the land.
series.futurist: A quarter of the world's population dies.

series.image: Martyrs under the altar: “How long?”
series.fulfilled: The blood of the prophets and saints is about to be avenged on that generation, as Jesus said (Matthew 23:35-36).
series.futurist: Tribulation martyrs waiting for vengeance.

series.image: Earthquake, darkened sun, falling stars; people call on the mountains to fall on them
series.fulfilled: Prophetic language for the collapse of a nation (Isaiah 13:10; 34:4). Jesus applied the cry to the mountains to Jerusalem's daughters (Luke 23:28-30).
series.futurist: Literal cosmic catastrophe near the end.

series.image: Silence in heaven; seven trumpets given
series.fulfilled: The prayers of the saints rise and fire is thrown on the land: the seventh seal opens into the trumpets.
series.futurist: The start of the trumpet judgements later in the tribulation.

series.image: Hail and fire mixed with blood; a third of the land burned
series.fulfilled: Roman scorched-earth campaigns through Galilee and Judea: villages and trees burned.
series.futurist: Literal fire burns a third of the earth's vegetation.

series.image: A great burning mountain thrown into the sea; a third of the sea becomes blood
series.fulfilled: Jesus spoke of “this mountain” being cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21). Josephus says the Sea of Galilee was red with blood after the battle at Tarichaeae.
series.futurist: A meteor or volcanic disaster poisons the oceans.

series.image: The star Wormwood makes the waters bitter
series.fulfilled: God promised to feed apostate Israel wormwood (Jeremiah 9:15; 23:15). The waters of the land turn bitter as judgement falls.
series.futurist: A comet or nuclear fallout poisons rivers.

series.image: A third of sun, moon and stars darkened
series.fulfilled: The prophets' picture of rulers falling (Isaiah 13:10; Ezekiel 32:7): the leaders of the nation are overthrown.
series.futurist: Literal dimming of the heavens.

series.image: Locusts from the abyss torment for five months
series.fulfilled: Demonic torment and frenzy in the land; five months fits, on some reckonings, the time from Florus' outrages in spring 66 to Cestius' advance in autumn. Joel's locust army is the background.
series.futurist: Demonic beings or modern war machines, sometimes identified with helicopters.

series.image: Four angels released at the Euphrates; a vast cavalry
series.fulfilled: Rome's armies gathered from the east: Josephus says Titus brought troops drawn from the Euphrates garrison to the siege.
series.futurist: An Asian army of two hundred million crosses the Euphrates.

series.image: The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord
series.fulfilled: With the old order judged, Christ's kingdom is openly established; God's temple in heaven is opened and the ark seen.
series.futurist: Christ's millennial kingdom announced at the end of the tribulation.

series.image: Painful sores on those with the mark of the beast
series.fulfilled: The boils of Egypt return on those who sided with the beast against the saints.
series.futurist: Literal sores on those who took a future mark.

series.image: The sea becomes blood like a corpse's
series.fulfilled: The slaughter at sea and on the lake, with the dead filling the water.
series.futurist: Every sea creature dies in the oceans.

series.image: Rivers turned to blood: “they shed the blood of saints, and you have given them blood to drink”
series.fulfilled: The fitting judgement on the city that killed the prophets (Matthew 23:35; Luke 11:50-51).
series.futurist: Fresh water turns to blood worldwide.

series.image: The sun scorches people with fire
series.fulfilled: Fire and fierce heat on the besieged; the burning of the city and temple.
series.futurist: Intense solar heat.

series.image: Darkness on the throne of the beast
series.fulfilled: Rome itself plunged into chaos: Nero's suicide in 68 and civil war in 69, ending with the Capitol burned.
series.futurist: Darkness on the Antichrist's capital.

series.image: The Euphrates dried; kings of the east; frog-like spirits gather them to Armageddon
series.fulfilled: The armies converging on Jerusalem; Megiddo recalls the great mourning of Zechariah 12:11 and Josiah's fall, a symbol of national disaster.
series.futurist: A literal final battle in the valley of Megiddo.

series.image: “It is done”; the great city split into three; hundred-pound hailstones
series.fulfilled: Josephus describes three factions dividing Jerusalem, and Roman catapults hurling white stones of a talent's weight.
series.futurist: Global earthquake and literal giant hail.

structures.name: Sequential
structures.summary: Twenty-one judgements one after another: seals, then trumpets, then bowls, through a future seven-year tribulation.
structures.strength: Follows the order in which John saw the visions.
structures.weakness: The sixth seal already brings the great day of wrath with the sky rolled up (6:12-17), yet many more judgements follow; the end comes several times.

structures.name: Recapitulation
structures.summary: The three series cover the same period, the whole time from Christ's first coming to his return, each from a new angle.
structures.holders: Many amillennial and idealist readers, from Victorinus and Augustine on
structures.strength: Explains why each series ends with the end, and why the trumpets and bowls mirror each other.
structures.weakness: Gives little weight to the escalation from a quarter to a third to the whole, and to the near time statements.

structures.name: Telescopic and escalating
structures.summary: The seventh seal opens into the seven trumpets, and the seventh trumpet into the seven bowls. The same war intensifies: a fourth, then a third, then all.
structures.holders: Many partial preterists and some futurists
structures.strength: Fits how the text links the series (8:1-2; 11:15; 15:1) and the rising fractions.
structures.weakness: Requires the series to overlap in time rather than follow neatly one after another.

exodus.note: The second trumpet and second and third bowls turn the waters to blood.
Three unclean spirits like frogs gather the kings.
Painful sores on the worshippers of the beast.
Hail mixed with fire; great hailstones at the last bowl.
Locusts from the abyss, fiercer than Egypt's.
A third of the lights darkened; darkness on the beast's throne.
Before the bowls, the victors sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb (15:3): a new exodus.

interludes.title: The 144,000 sealed
interludes.reading: Before the winds of judgement blow on the land, a remnant from the tribes of Israel is sealed: the Jewish believers who fled Jerusalem, as Jesus warned (Luke 21:20-21).

interludes.title: A multitude from every nation
interludes.reading: John hears a number from Israel and sees a countless multitude from all nations: the one people of God, safe through the great tribulation.

interludes.title: The little scroll: no more delay
interludes.reading: An angel swears there will be no more delay (10:6); John must prophesy again about many peoples.

interludes.title: The temple measured; the two witnesses
interludes.reading: The temple still stands to be measured; the holy city is trampled for forty-two months. The witnesses die in “the great city where their Lord was crucified” (11:8).

interludes.title: The woman, the dragon and the beasts
interludes.reading: The story behind the judgements: the Messiah's birth and ascension, Satan cast down, the church protected in the wilderness, and the beasts who make war on the saints.

symbols.name: The beast from the sea
symbols.fulfilled: Rome, and especially Nero, who made war on the saints for about forty-two months (AD 64-68).
symbols.futurist: A future world ruler, the Antichrist.

symbols.name: The number 666
symbols.fulfilled: “Nero Caesar” written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666; the ancient variant 616 matches the Latin spelling.
symbols.futurist: The name or mark of the future Antichrist.

symbols.name: The beast from the land
symbols.fulfilled: The false prophet: the imperial cult's priesthood in Asia, or the Jewish leaders who sided with Rome against the church (John 19:15).
symbols.futurist: A future religious leader who promotes the Antichrist.

symbols.name: The mark on hand and forehead
symbols.fulfilled: A mirror of the law bound on hand and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:8): allegiance shown in deeds and mind, and the economic pressure on those who would not bow.
symbols.futurist: A literal mark or technology required for buying and selling.

symbols.name: Babylon the harlot
symbols.fulfilled: Many partial preterists read her as apostate Jerusalem, drunk with the blood of the prophets (18:24; Matthew 23:35); others read her as Rome on seven hills.
symbols.futurist: A future world religious and economic system.

symbols.name: Seven kings: five fallen, one is
symbols.fulfilled: The Caesars: Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Caligula and Claudius fallen; Nero reigning as John wrote; Galba to reign briefly.
symbols.futurist: Seven empires through history, the last still future.

symbols.name: The woman clothed with the sun
symbols.fulfilled: The faithful people of God, who bore the Messiah and fled into the wilderness for 1,260 days.

symbols.name: 42 months / 1,260 days
symbols.fulfilled: The length of the Roman war against Jerusalem (spring 67 to August 70), and of Nero's persecution (late 64 to mid 68).
symbols.futurist: Each half of the seven-year tribulation.

symbols.name: Armageddon
symbols.fulfilled: “Mount Megiddo,” a symbol of national catastrophe and mourning (Zechariah 12:11), gathering the armies against Jerusalem.
symbols.futurist: A literal last battle in northern Israel.

symbols.name: The rider on the white horse
symbols.fulfilled: Christ conquering by his word (the sword from his mouth), judging the beast and false prophet.
symbols.futurist: The visible second coming at the end of the tribulation.

symbols.name: The thousand years
symbols.fulfilled: Christ's present reign with his saints, Satan bound so that the nations may hear the gospel; the final rebellion and judgement still ahead.
symbols.futurist: A future earthly kingdom after the return.

problems.name: Bookends ignored
problems.problem: Revelation opens and closes with “soon” and “the time is near.” Daniel was told to seal his book because the time was far off; John is told not to seal his because it was near. Pushing the judgements thousands of years ahead reverses that contrast.
problems.reply: Read the bookends plainly: the judgements were near to John's readers.

problems.name: A letter to the wrong readers
problems.problem: Revelation was sent to seven real churches facing real persecution. If its judgements were two thousand years away, its comfort and warnings meant nothing to them.
problems.reply: The judgements answered the martyrs' “How long?” in their own day.

problems.name: Literal when convenient
problems.problem: The two hundred million horsemen are taken as a literal army, but locusts with human faces and lions' teeth become helicopters. The method changes from verse to verse.
problems.reply: Read Revelation consistently as a book of signs (1:1), drawing its images from the prophets.

problems.name: The end, again and again
problems.problem: On a strictly sequential reading, the sixth seal already rolls up the sky and brings the great day of wrath, yet fourteen more judgements follow on the same earth.
problems.reply: Prophetic “cosmic” language describes the fall of a nation, and the series overlap and escalate.

problems.name: A temple that has to be rebuilt
problems.problem: John is told to measure the temple and its worshippers (11:1-2). A futurist reading has to supply a third temple the text does not mention.
problems.reply: The temple was standing when John wrote, and the city was trampled for forty-two months.

problems.name: Changing identifications
problems.problem: Wormwood has been Chernobyl, the locusts helicopters, the kings of the east China. Each generation fits the judgements to its headlines, and each identification has had to be replaced.
problems.reply: Begin with what the images meant in the prophets and to John's readers.

problems.name: A rapture read into 4:1
problems.problem: “Come up here” is spoken to John alone, to show him a vision. Reading it as the rapture of the church before the judgements has no basis in the text.
problems.reply: John is taken up in the Spirit to see, and the saints remain through the tribulation (7:14; 13:7).

problems.name: No agreed map
problems.problem: Historicist writers have matched the trumpets to the Goths, the Vandals, the Saracens, the Turks and more, and rarely agree with each other. A key that opens every lock opens none.
problems.reply: The text gives its own key: the near time and the city where the Lord was crucified.

problems.name: The day-for-a-year principle
problems.problem: Turning 1,260 days into 1,260 years led to many failed dates, from the 1260s to 1798 and 1866.
problems.reply: Forty-two months is a literal or symbolic short period, half of Daniel's week.

problems.name: No particular time or place
problems.problem: Idealism rightly draws timeless lessons, but it cannot explain the concrete markers: a standing temple, “the great city where their Lord was crucified,” five kings fallen and one reigning.
problems.reply: Revelation's lessons are timeless because its first fulfilment was real.

problems.name: The last judgement made past
problems.problem: Full preterism places the resurrection and great white throne in AD 70, but Paul condemns saying the resurrection has already happened.
problems.reply: Revelation 20:7-15 looks beyond the first-century judgements to the end of history.

problems.name: Ignoring the internal date
problems.problem: Many readers assume a date of about AD 95 from one ambiguous sentence of Irenaeus, while the book itself shows the temple standing and the sixth king reigning.
problems.reply: Let the book's own evidence weigh most; see the dating study.

objections.q: Wasn't Revelation written around AD 95, after Jerusalem fell?
objections.a: That date rests mainly on a sentence in Irenaeus that can be read as saying John was seen, not the vision, in Domitian's time. Revelation itself shows the temple standing (11:1-2) and the sixth king reigning (17:10), and never mentions the fall of Jerusalem, which would have been a powerful example. Many scholars hold an early date of about AD 65-68.

objections.q: Doesn't the language describe a global catastrophe?
objections.a: The word often translated “earth” also means “land,” as when “all the tribes of the land” mourn over the one they pierced (1:7; Zechariah 12:10-12). The prophets used cosmic language for the fall of Babylon, Egypt and Edom (Isaiah 13; 34; Ezekiel 32).

objections.q: If Babylon is Jerusalem, why the seven hills?
objections.a: The beast she rides is Rome on its seven hills; the harlot is carried by it, as Jerusalem's leaders allied with Rome against Christ (“We have no king but Caesar,” John 19:15). Some partial preterists do read the harlot as Rome itself.

objections.q: The judgements say people did not repent. Doesn't that mean the whole world?
objections.a: The same refusal is said of the land's people throughout Jesus' ministry (Matthew 11:20-24). The judgements fall on those who chose the beast, while the sealed servants are protected.

objections.q: Isn't matching verses to Josephus just guesswork?
objections.a: Some matches are closer than others, and partial preterists should hold them loosely. But the overall pattern of war, famine, factional slaughter, the temple burned and the city split into three is well documented, and the main point does not depend on any single detail.

objections.q: Does this reading deny Christ's second coming?
objections.a: No. Partial preterists read some “comings” in Revelation as Christ coming in judgement on that generation, as the prophets spoke of the LORD coming on the clouds against Egypt (Isaiah 19:1). They confess his future bodily return, the resurrection and the final judgement.

objections.q: Doesn't 1:7 say every eye will see him?
objections.a: It says “even those who pierced him” and “all the tribes of the land,” quoting Zechariah 12 about Jerusalem's mourning. Jesus told the high priest he would see the Son of Man coming on the clouds (Matthew 26:64).

objections.q: If the judgements are past, what about chapters 20-22?
objections.a: Revelation moves from the judgement on the old order to the reign of Christ, the final rebellion and the last judgement, and the new creation. Partial preterists see the thousand-year reign as now, and the great white throne and full new creation as still to come.

groups.title: How the judgements fit together
groups.summary: Sequence, recapitulation, or a telescope that escalates.

groups.title: The seals
groups.summary: The four horsemen, the martyrs and the great day of wrath.

groups.title: The trumpets and bowls
groups.summary: Plagues of a new exodus, matched with the war of AD 66-70.

groups.title: Figures and symbols
groups.summary: The beast, 666, Babylon, Armageddon and the thousand years.

groups.title: Reading Revelation well
groups.summary: Time, audience and the prophets' language.

questions.q: Why are there three series of seven?
questions.short: Seven is the number of completeness, and the Law threatened Israel with judgement “seven times” for covenant breaking. The three series escalate from a quarter to a third to all.
questions.answer: Leviticus 26 warns four times that God will punish his people “seven times” for their sins (26:18, 21, 24, 28). Revelation's sevens echo that covenant curse. The fractions grow: the fourth seal reaches a quarter of the land, the trumpets a third, and the bowls everything. The seventh seal opens into the trumpets, and the seventh trumpet into the bowls, so the same judgement intensifies.
examples: Leviticus 26:18: I will discipline you again sevenfold for your sins.
Revelation 6:8: a fourth; 8:7-12: a third; 16:3: every living thing in the sea.
questions.other: Recapitulation readers see three views of the same whole church age; sequential readers see twenty-one events in order.

questions.q: Who are the judgements aimed at?
questions.short: Those who “dwell on the land” and persecuted the saints. The judgements answer the martyrs' cry, “How long before you avenge our blood?”
questions.answer: The fifth seal shows martyrs crying for vengeance on “those who dwell on the land.” The third bowl explains: they shed the blood of saints and prophets, and God gives them blood to drink. Jesus had said that all the righteous blood from Abel to Zechariah would come on his generation (Matthew 23:35-36), and that the days of vengeance were coming on Jerusalem (Luke 21:22).
examples: Revelation 6:10: avenge our blood on those who dwell on the land.
Revelation 16:6: they have shed the blood of saints and prophets.
Revelation 18:24: in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints.
questions.other: Futurists see the judgements falling on the whole unbelieving world in the future.

questions.short: Conquest, war, famine and death: the four judgements Ezekiel threatened on Jerusalem, released in the war of AD 66-70.
questions.answer: Zechariah saw coloured horses patrolling the earth. Ezekiel names God's four sore judgements on Jerusalem: sword, famine, wild beasts and pestilence. Revelation's riders bring conquest, bloodshed, famine prices and death over a fourth of the land. Josephus describes all of these in the war and siege.
examples: Ezekiel 14:21: my four disastrous acts of judgement on Jerusalem.
Revelation 6:6: a quart of wheat for a denarius, a day's wage.
questions.other: Futurists see the riders as the opening judgements of the future tribulation; idealists as recurring patterns of history.

questions.q: Is the sixth seal the end of the world?
questions.short: It uses the prophets' language for the fall of a nation, and its cry to the mountains is the one Jesus put in the mouths of Jerusalem's people.
questions.answer: Isaiah used darkened sun and falling stars for the fall of Babylon (13:10) and the sky rolled up like a scroll for Edom (34:4). On the way to the cross, Jesus told the women of Jerusalem that days were coming when they would say to the mountains, “Fall on us.” The sixth seal is that day.
examples: Isaiah 34:4: the skies roll up like a scroll (against Edom).
Luke 23:30: they will begin to say to the mountains, “Fall on us.”
questions.other: Futurists read the sixth seal as literal cosmic upheaval shortly before Christ's return.

questions.q: Why do the trumpets and bowls copy the plagues of Egypt?
questions.short: Because Jerusalem had become “Egypt.” Revelation calls it the great city “symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.”
questions.answer: Blood, frogs, boils, hail, locusts and darkness return. Before the bowls are poured, the saints sing the song of Moses. The message is a new exodus: God brings his people out, and the persecuting city receives Egypt's plagues. The table on this page lines up each plague with its trumpet and bowl.
examples: Revelation 11:8: symbolically called Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified.
Revelation 15:3: the song of Moses and of the Lamb.
questions.other: Futurists see the plagues as literal repetitions of Egypt's on a world scale.

questions.q: Why do the trumpets and bowls follow the same order?
questions.short: Both hit the land, the sea, the rivers, the heavenly lights, the darkness, the Euphrates and the air, in that order. The bowls complete what the trumpets began.
questions.answer: Trumpet and bowl one strike the land; two, the sea; three, rivers and springs; four, the sun; five, darkness and torment; six, the Euphrates; seven, the final announcement with lightning, earthquake and hail. The trumpets reach a third; the bowls are total. Tap “show parallels” on the board to see them line up.
examples: Trumpet 2 and bowl 2: the sea becomes blood.
Trumpet 6 and bowl 6: the Euphrates.
questions.other: Recapitulation readers take the parallels as evidence that the two series describe the same period.

questions.q: What is the great city split into three parts?
questions.short: On this reading, Jerusalem, divided between three warring factions during the siege, as Josephus records.
questions.answer: Revelation's “great city” is identified in 11:8 as the place where the Lord was crucified. During the siege, Jerusalem was held by three rival leaders, John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar son of Simon, who fought each other while the Romans attacked. The last bowl also has hailstones of about a talent; Josephus says the Romans' catapults hurled white stones of a talent's weight.
examples: Josephus, Jewish War 5.1: the city divided into three factions.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.6.3: stones of a talent's weight.
questions.other: Others read the great city as Rome or as a future world capital.

questions.short: Written in Hebrew letters, “Nero Caesar” adds up to 666; and the ancient manuscripts that read 616 match the Latin spelling “Nero Caesar.”
questions.answer: In Hebrew and Greek, letters double as numbers. The Hebrew spelling of Nero Caesar (nrwn qsr) totals 666. Irenaeus already knew copies that read 616, which fits the Latin form “Nero” without the final n. Nero persecuted Christians from AD 64 until his death in 68, about forty-two months, and was the sixth emperor, the one who “is” in 17:10.
examples: Revelation 13:18: let the one who has understanding calculate the number.
Revelation 13:5: authority for forty-two months.
questions.other: Futurists say no past figure fully fits, and that the number awaits a future Antichrist.

questions.short: Partial preterists are divided: many say apostate Jerusalem, which killed the prophets; others say pagan Rome on its seven hills.
questions.answer: The case for Jerusalem: she is drunk with the blood of the saints, in her was found the blood of the prophets (18:24, echoing Matthew 23:35), she is called a harlot as Israel was by the prophets (Ezekiel 16), and she rides the beast as Jerusalem's leaders relied on Caesar. The case for Rome: seven hills, a city that rules the kings of the earth (17:18). Either way, she fell in that era.
examples: Ezekiel 16:15: you played the whore.
Revelation 18:24: in her was found the blood of prophets.
questions.other: Futurists see a future world religion or a rebuilt Babylon.

questions.q: Is Armageddon a future world war?
questions.short: The name means “mountain of Megiddo,” a place that stood for national disaster and mourning. In Revelation it is the gathering of the armies against the beloved city.
questions.answer: Megiddo is a plain, not a mountain, so the name is symbolic. Josiah fell there, and Zechariah compares Jerusalem's mourning over the pierced one to the mourning in the plain of Megiddo (12:11). In the sixth bowl, unclean spirits gather the kings for the great day of God: the armies that came against Jerusalem.
examples: 2 Kings 23:29: Josiah killed at Megiddo.
Zechariah 12:11: as great as the mourning at Megiddo.
questions.other: Futurists expect a literal final battle in the Jezreel valley.

questions.q: How should we read Revelation's images?
questions.short: As a book of signs (1:1) whose pictures come from the Old Testament prophets, written to real churches about things soon to happen.
questions.answer: Revelation has hundreds of allusions to the Old Testament and almost no direct quotations; its images are borrowed from Exodus, Daniel, Ezekiel, Zechariah and Isaiah. Ask what each picture meant there. Then ask what it would mean to seven churches in Asia under Nero, told that the time was near. Finally, apply its lasting truths: Christ reigns, persecutors fall, the faithful are kept.
examples: Revelation 1:1: he made it known (literally signified) by his angel.
Revelation 1:11: write what you see and send it to the seven churches.
questions.other: Idealists stress the lasting truths; futurists the final fulfilment; historicists the course of church history.

questions.q: Why does it matter which view we take?
questions.short: It decides whether Revelation is fear about the future or comfort from the past and present: Christ has already judged the persecutors and reigns now.
questions.answer: If the judgements are all future, Christians tend to read the news anxiously and expect to escape before the worst. If they were fulfilled, Revelation shows the Lamb who keeps his word, vindicates his martyrs and reigns over the kings of the earth now (1:5), and it calls believers to faithful witness in every age.
examples: Revelation 1:5: the ruler of kings on earth.
Revelation 12:11: they conquered by the blood of the Lamb and the word of their testimony.
questions.other: Futurists answer that their view also centres on the Lamb's victory, and gives urgency to evangelism.

nodes.help: Weigh 11:1-2 (the temple measured) and 17:10 (the sixth king reigns).

nodes.q: Do “soon” and “near” mean near to John's readers?

options.label: No, they mean sudden or certain

nodes.q: Does Revelation 20:11-15 describe a judgement still future?

options.label: No, it was all fulfilled by AD 70

nodes.q: Do the visions map church history age by age?
nodes.help: Historicists read the trumpets as invasions of the Roman empire and beyond.

results.title: Partial preterist
results.text: The seals, trumpets and bowls fell on that generation; Christ reigns now; his return, the resurrection and the last judgement are still ahead. This is the reading this study follows.

results.title: Full preterist
results.text: Everything, including the resurrection and final judgement, was fulfilled by AD 70. This view is outside the historic creeds.

results.title: Futurist
results.text: Most of chapters 4-22 describe a future tribulation, the second coming and the millennium.

results.title: Historicist
results.text: Revelation is a map of church history from the apostles to the end.

results.title: Idealist
results.text: Revelation pictures the timeless conflict of Christ and his people with evil.

quiz.q: How many judgements are there in the three series?
quiz.explain: Seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls.

quiz.q: What fraction do the trumpets strike?
quiz.explain: Revelation 8:7-12. The fourth seal reached a fourth; the bowls reach everything.

quiz.q: Which Old Testament event do the trumpets and bowls echo most?
quiz.explain: Blood, frogs, boils, hail, locusts and darkness.

quiz.q: What does Revelation 11:8 call the great city?
options: Sodom and Egypt, where their Lord was crucified

quiz.q: Whose words does the sixth seal's cry to the mountains repeat?
options: Jesus to the women of Jerusalem

quiz.q: What does “Nero Caesar” total in Hebrew letters?
quiz.explain: The Latin spelling gives 616, the ancient variant.
